lesson.title: The Reagan Revolution: A New Conservative Coalition Takes Power
lesson.summary: Ronald Reagan's landslide victory in 1980 brought a confident new conservative coalition to power in Washington, built on the frustrations of a decade of economic stagnation and the humiliation of the Iranian hostage crisis.
lesson.body:
Ronald Reagan, a former Hollywood actor and two term governor of California, defeated incumbent President Jimmy Carter in the November 1980 election by a landslide, winning 44 of 50 states. Reagan's victory reflected years of frustration that had built up over the course of the 1970s: the stagflation that had eroded Americans' standard of living, the sense of national weakness reinforced by the ongoing Iranian hostage crisis, and a broader feeling that the federal government had grown too large and too intrusive without solving the problems it claimed to address.

Reagan built his victory on a coalition that brought together several strands of American conservatism that had not always worked closely together before. Economic conservatives wanted lower taxes, less regulation, and a smaller federal government. Social conservatives, energized by religious organizations like Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority, wanted the government to take conservative positions on issues like abortion and school prayer. Anti communist hawks wanted a more assertive foreign policy and a stronger military after what they saw as a decade of American retreat. Reagan also drew support from many working class and union voters, often called Reagan Democrats, who were drawn to his message of national pride and economic opportunity even though they had traditionally voted for Democratic candidates.

In his first inaugural address on January 20, 1981, delivered the same day the Iranian hostages were finally released, Reagan captured the spirit of his movement with the line that in the present crisis, government was not the solution to the country's problems but was itself the problem. Just weeks later, on March 30, 1981, Reagan survived an assassination attempt by John Hinckley Jr. outside a Washington hotel, and his composure and good humor during his recovery boosted his popularity and gave his young administration a sense of momentum.

Reagan's presidency set out to reverse the direction of federal policy since the New Deal and Great Society eras, pursuing large tax cuts, reduced regulation, a major military buildup, and a more confrontational stance toward the Soviet Union, an agenda that came to be called the Reagan Revolution. The specific economic program built around tax cuts and deregulation became known as supply side economics or Reaganomics, and it would shape American economic policy debates for decades to come.
